content.text: •begins in distal arteries/veins → progresses to more proximal arterial occlusive dz
Sus in young smokers/tobacco users w/ dist extremity ischemia/ischemic ulcers or gangrene of the digits
•MC seen in young men 20-45yrs esp. in India, Asia, & the Middle East
dist extremity ischemia both upper & lower extremities
(claud in the lower calf or arch of the foot, ischemic ulcers),
– ← ↓blood flow in the medium & sm arteries and veins
Abnorm Allen test: delayed perf of the radial ulnar arteries
Wound care—debridement, moist dressings, (−) P wound therapy
Amputation if gangrene occurs or to ⍉the spread of infect in severe ischemic cases
: PG analog that may help w/ critical limb ischemia while smoke cessation = in progress
▪︎fever, strawberry red tongue, LAD, rash, conjunctivitis, erythema + edema of hands + feet
▪︎oral mucous membrane changes (injected or fissured lips, injected pharynx, strawberry tongue)
▪︎peripheral extremity changes (erythema of palms or soles, edema of hands or feet, periungual desquamation)
: b/c many are pedunculated, some can cause a
“ball-valve” obstruct of the mitral orifice, mimicking MS
Dyspnea, wt loss & syncope (from MV obstruct)
Triad of embolic phenomenon, mitral stenosis-like sxs & constitutional “flu-like” sxs (fever, wt loss)
▪︎ECG: peaked T wave → dropped P wave → widened QRS → sine wave
▪︎membrane stabilization: calcium gluconate or chloride (immediate, 30–60 min)
▪︎redistribution: insulin (20–30 min, 4–6 hr; shifts K into cell), albuterol (15–30 min, 2–4 hr; ⇡cAMP + shifts K into cells), sodium bicarbonate (less effective; 5–10 min, 1–2 hr)

▪︎elimination: furosemide (15–30 min, 2–3 hr; ⇡renal K excretion), enteral cation exchange resins — patiromer (adults), sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (adults), sodium polystyrene (no longer recommended in adults) (1–4 hr, 4–6 hr; CI preterm infants, small or large bowel obstruction, ileus, postop pts), hemodialysis (immediate, 2–6 hr)
▪︎ECG progression: flattening of T wave → ST-T flattening (sometimes slight ST depression) + U wave → ST depression more noticeable + U wave ⇡amplitude until U wave overtakes T wave
▪︎acute = developed <48 hrs; chronic = ≥48 hrs or unknown
▪︎acute → treat in hospital; Sx → 100 mL bolus 3% saline, repeat twice more PRN, monitor Na hourly until ⇡4–6 mEq/L
▪︎chronic w/ severe Sx or known intracranial pathology → inpatient 100 mL 3% bolus; Na <120 → inpatient
▪︎self-induced water intoxication → general measures, monitor Na q6–12h
▪︎edematous → 3% saline 15–30 mL/hr + IV furosemide (≥40 mg) BID, target ⇡4–6 mEq/L per 24 hr, stop when Na ≥125
▪︎high risk for osmotic demyelination (Na ≤105, hypoK, alcohol use d/o, malnourished, liver dz) → 3% saline 15–30 mL/hr + IV/SC desmopressin 1–2 mcg q6–8h
▪︎Osborn wave (J wave) — not pathognomonic; clinical most prominent in precordial leads; size correlates w/ degree of hypothermia; usually resolves w/ warming; no prognostic value
▪︎J wave etiology: hypothermia (<32°C / 90°F), normal variant, hypercalcemia, neurological insult, medications, VF
▪︎Trousseau sign = carpopedal spasm from inflating BP cuff above SBP ×3 min — thumb adduction, MCP flexion, IP extension, wrist flexion
▪︎Chvostek sign = contraction of ipsilateral facial muscles tapping facial nerve just anterior to ear — twitching of lip to spasm of all facial muscles
